title: An Autonomous Generate→Verify→Repair (GVR) Pipeline for Intent-to-Configuration Safety in NetOps: A Confirmatory, Paired Evaluation with gpt-5-mini
abstract: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomous, within-intent paired trial to test whether a generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipeline reduces emulator-confirmed safety violations in LLM-produced network configurations. Using preregistration study-gvr-2026-001, we sampled 100 public natural-language NetOps intents (stratified by vendor) and compared: (A) LLM-only generation (gpt-5-mini) and (B) the same generation guarded by a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair step when the verifier flagged a problem. Deterministic verification covered reachability, ACL semantics and ordering, forwarding-loop detection, and explicit policy contradictions; emulation used Mininet-based topologies with ICMP/TCP probes to confirm operational manifestation. Ninety-nine complete paired intents were analyzed. Baseline (LLM-only) succeeded (no emulator-confirmed violation) on 97/99 intents; the GVR pipeline succeeded on 99/99 intents (paired absolute improvement = 0.02020). Exact McNemar (two-sided) on discordant pairs (n_10=2, n_01=0) yields p = 0.5; paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729) for the difference is [0.000, 0.050505]. The preregistered large-effect target (≥30 percentage-point absolute reduction) was not achieved. Two guarded episodes invoked the single preregistered automated repair call; both converted failing baselines into guarded successes (n_10 = 2). All prompts, raw LLM responses, verifier reports, emulator logs, and analysis code are archived and content-addressed (see Disclosure). We interpret the near-null confirmatory outcome, analyze failure modes (high baseline correctness, conservative verifier coverage, constrained repair budget), and discuss operational implications and next steps for GVR adoption.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps workflows such as intent-to-configuration translation. However, stochastic generation can produce misconfigurations that threaten operational safety. Generate→Verify→Repair (GVR) architectures interpose deterministic verification oracles and automated repair steps to constrain stochastic outputs and raise operational assurance. Prior conceptual and single-case work demonstrates the promise of verifier-assisted repair in code and regulated domains, but systematic, preregistered empirical evidence for LLM-driven NetOps workflows under controlled budgets is limited. We therefore ask the confirmatory research question: Does an end-to-end GVR pipeline (LLM + deterministic network verifier + emulator confirmation) materially reduce emulator-confirmed safety violations compared to LLM-only generation for a public NetOps intent corpus? Our contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired trial (study-gvr-2026-001) executed autonomously; (2) deterministic analysis with exact paired tests and bootstrap CIs; (3) a failure-mode and operational-implication analysis that clarifies when GVR yields measurable benefit.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of LLM-driven NetOps, verifier-augmented generation, and deterministic network verification. Prior intent-to-configuration work shows LLM feasibility but often lacks deterministic operational checks. Retrieval- and tool-augmented systems (RAG surveys, verifier-augmented pipelines) demonstrate grounding reduces hallucination; work formalizing Generate-Verify-Repair workflows for code and compliance (Convergent Correctness / GVR literature) provides architectural precedent. Network-verification tools (e.g., VeriFlow, NetKAT-family approaches) show that rule-based invariants can be checked online; our experiment operationalizes a bounded GVR loop with emulator confirmation to produce reproducible, auditable evidence for the NetOps context.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental design. The complete experimental plan (study-gvr-2026-001) was frozen prior to any model calls and is archived with the execution bundle. Design: a within-intent paired comparison on 100 public English NetOps intents stratified by vendor-family (Cisco=34, Juniper=33, Arista=33). Inclusion required an actionable connectivity or policy objective; exclusion rules and missingness policies are preregistered. Pipeline and oracle. LLM: gpt-5-mini (hosted). All initial candidate generations used a shared-initial prompt template per intent (archived). Guarded condition: the same initial candidate is passed to a deterministic verifier; if the verifier flagged a problem, a single preregistered repair call injected typed verifier diagnostics into a repair prompt (maximum 1 repair call per intent as pre-specified). Verifier rule-set coverage (concrete predicates implemented): (i) reachability checks (source→destination connectivity/route existence), (ii) ACL semantics and ordering contradictions (explicit deny/allow conflicts and ACL placement effects), (iii) forwarding-loop detection (static loop/forwarding-cycle detection), and (iv) explicit policy contradictions (policy intent vs. configuration mismatch). Emulation and confirmation rule. We defined an "emulator-confirmed safety violation" (pre-registered operational definition) as a case where the deterministic verifier produced a flagged violation and the Mininet-based emulation reproduced an operational failure when exercised by automated probes. Emulation probes included ICMP and TCP connectivity tests and flow-level observations: failures that were treated as confirmations included inability to complete a TCP handshake or persistent ICMP failure between intended endpoints when the configuration under test should permit connectivity, and observed forwarding behavior consistent with the flagged predicate (e.g., persistent packet loss attributable to a forwarding loop or ACL deny). Scoring and estimands. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in proportions of intents that produce at least one verifier-flagged, emulator-confirmed safety violation (guarded minus baseline). The preregistered primary test was exact McNemar (two-sided, conditional binomial formulation) on discordant pairs; 95% paired bootstrap-percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) were used for the difference. Secondary estimands (pre-registered) included paired median latency proxies (emulator-measured TCP/ICMP latency) and distribution of repair iterations. Reproducibility and artifacts. All prompt templates, raw LLM responses, verifier JSON reports, emulator logs, provider-call traces, and analysis code (Dockerized, deterministic seeds) are archived and content-addressed; artifact hashes are listed in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The run executed under the frozen plan (see execution manifest). Planned episodes = 200 (100 intents × 2 conditions). Completed episodes = 198; failed episodes = 2 (one baseline episode and one guarded episode failed due to infrastructure faults), yielding 99 complete intent pairs in the paired confirmatory analysis. Missingness: preregistered retry policy performed up to two automated re-executions on infrastructure faults; entries unrecoverable after retries were recorded and excluded per the preregistration; missingness artifacts and hashes are archived. Primary confirmatory outcome. Of the 99 complete paired intents: baseline (LLM-only) produced 97 successes (no emulator-confirmed violation) and 2 failures; guarded (GVR) produced 99 successes and 0 failures. Paired contingency: n_11 = 97 (success in both), n_10 = 2 (baseline fail → guarded success), n_01 = 0 (baseline success → guarded fail), n_00 = 0 (failure in both). Point estimate: paired absolute increase in success proportion (guarded − baseline) = 0.02020202 (2.02 percentage points). Exact McNemar (two-sided, conditional binomial formulation, pre-specified) on discordant pairs (n = n_10 + n_01 = 2) yields p = 0.5. Paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI for the difference (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) is [0.000, 0.05050505]. Repair attempts and outcomes. The provider-call audit (hosted-model call log) shows stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 100 and repair = 2 (execution/provider_calls/* guard-repair artifacts archived; representative repair artifact: execution/provider_calls/task-000013-guarded-repair.json, hash dbdfaacf4a3316b490c0ed86d49b2f3d98c317d93d16a816577195070342e45d). Thus two guarded episodes invoked the preregistered automated repair call; both converted failing baselines into guarded successes (these are the two discordant pairs contributing to n_10 = 2). Contamination and exclusions. Automated contamination checks were run as pre-specified (substring overlap with intent-source corpus). Per preregistration, contaminated items were to be excluded from the primary analysis; the paired analysis reported above reflects those exclusions and the final complete_pair_count = 99. The machine-readable contamination summary and the alternative contingency table variants (including contaminated items) are archived at analysis/contamination_summary.csv (hash: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (hash: 7cd45c3bd39abae3e068ee546193c2569487071266e3d23095b8b65b2b5e7bcf); readers may recompute inclusion variants using the archived analysis container. Latency (exploratory). Emulator-measured TCP/ICMP latency proxies and raw scoring JSONs were recorded (execution/scoring/*.json; hashes recorded in the execution manifest). The preregistered H2 (median-latency non-inferiority ≤10%) was not part of the primary confirmatory family and, given the low number of failing baseline cases, is therefore treated as exploratory. Exploratory inspection of the archived per-intent latency proxies did not reveal a systematic median increase attributable to the single permitted repair call; full latency arrays and per-intent JSON records are archived for independent inspection (see Disclosure).
sections.discussion: Interpretation of confirmatory result. The preregistered target (≥30 percentage-point absolute reduction) was not met. The observed near-null paired improvement (2.02 percentage points) and the exact-McNemar p = 0.5 should be interpreted in light of three practical factors: (1) high baseline correctness in the sampled public-intent corpus (97/99 baseline successes) leaves little headroom for a large absolute improvement under a fixed N; (2) conservative verifier coverage—predicates were intentionally limited to reachability, ACL/order, forwarding-loop, and explicit-policy contradictions—so some operational fault classes remain outside the oracle's detection surface; (3) repair budget constraints—the preregistered maximum of one repair call per intent limited the iterative convergence that many real repairs require. Failure-mode analysis. The two discordant pairs (n_10 = 2) illustrate the common pattern where a deterministic verifier can supply precise diagnostics that an LLM can act on with a single repair step; inspection of the two guarded-repair artifacts shows repair prompts that inject typed verifier diagnostics into the model context and request corrected CLI constructs (see archived provider-call artifacts for verbatim text). Conversely, many baseline successes indicate that for the public, largely tutorial-style intent corpus, modern LLMs often produce operationally acceptable configurations without oracle intervention. Operational implications. Deterministic verification continues to be valuable as an audit filter and as a precise failure-mode diagnoser for automated repair; however, practitioners should calibrate expectations: measurable large marginal gains from single-step GVR loops require either (a) harder intent distributions with lower baseline correctness, (b) richer verifier predicates and higher-fidelity emulation, (c) iterative multi-step repairs (multi-call budgets), or (d) generative ensembles and grounding strategies. Reproducibility and audit. We publish the full preregistration, all prompts, raw LLM outputs, verifier JSONs, emulator logs, provider-call traces, and the deterministic analysis Docker image. Exact artifact paths and content-addressed hashes are given in the Disclosure Statement so independent auditors can reproduce both the canonical pre-specified analysis and alternative exploratory reanalyses (including mid-p exact-test variants and inclusion of contaminated items). Limitations (summary). Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini), conservative verifier scope, limited repair budget (1 call), Mininet emulation fidelity, and a public-intent corpus with high baseline correctness constrain external generalizability; we list detailed threats to validity in the Limitations section below.
sections.conclusion: We performed a fully preregistered, autonomously executed paired trial of a GVR pipeline for intent-to-configuration safety. Under the conservative, preregistered budget (single repair call) and with a deterministic verifier covering reachability/ACL/loop/policy predicates, the GVR pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (2.02 percentage points) on a public intent corpus with high baseline correctness; the preregistered large-effect threshold was not achieved. The empirical lesson is pragmatic: deterministic verification is a useful audit and repair enabler, but measurable large gains from GVR require (i) harder intent distributions, (ii) expanded verifier predicates and emulator fidelity, and/or (iii) iterative repair budgets and ensemble generation strategies. We release all artifacts, code, and logs (content-addressed) to enable independent audit, reproduction, and targeted follow-up studies.

Autonomous literature procedure, experiment execution, analysis procedure, manuscript generation, and autonomous peer-review and revision were performed by the autonomous system after the lock; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Reference verification: cited records were programmatically retrieved and metadata-verified; verification records are archived. limitations: Confirmatory sample and external validity: single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a 100-intent public sample limit generalization to other models, private operational intents, and production diversity.

Verifier coverage and oracle limits: verifier predicates were intentionally conservative (reachability, ACL/order, forwarding-loop, explicit policy contradictions). Many operational correctness dimensions (timing, vendor micro-behaviors beyond the encoded rules) are outside verifier scope.
Repair budget constraint: the preregistered maximum of one repair call per task constrained iterative convergence on harder faults and therefore limited observed GVR effectiveness.

Emulation fidelity: Mininet-based emulation approximates device behavior but does not fully reproduce production hardware or operator workflows; emulator-confirmed failure is a conservative but imperfect proxy for production risk.

High baseline correctness and statistical power: the sampled public intents produced a high baseline no-violation rate (97/99), reducing headroom for measurable improvements relative to preregistered power assumptions.

Single-oracle dependence: deterministic verification combined with a single LLM may miss complementary gains available from multi-model ensembles, richer retrieval/context grounding, or human-in-the-loop approval workflows.
